Fit the Skellam Distribution to a Sample

Source: R/skellam.fit.R
skellam.fit.Rd

Estimates the rates \((\lambda_1, \lambda_2)\) of a Skellam distribution from a sample of differences of counts, by maximum likelihood (default) or by the method of moments, and returns a fitted-model object that works with the usual extractor functions.

Usage

skellam.fit(x, method = c("mle", "moments"), na.rm = FALSE)

# S3 method for class 'skellam_fit'
print(x, digits = max(3L, getOption("digits") - 3L), ...)

# S3 method for class 'skellam_fit'
summary(object, level = 0.95, ...)

# S3 method for class 'skellam_fit'
coef(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'skellam_fit'
vcov(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'skellam_fit'
logLik(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'skellam_fit'
nobs(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'skellam_fit'
confint(object, parm, level = 0.95, ...)

# S3 method for class 'skellam_fit'
predict(object, x, type = c("pmf", "cdf", "quantile"), p, ...)

# S3 method for class 'skellam_fit'
simulate(object, nsim = 1, seed = NULL, ...)

Arguments

x

A numeric vector of integers (differences of counts; any sign).

method

"mle" (default) for maximum likelihood, or "moments" for the method-of-moments estimates \(\lambda_1 = (s^2 + \bar x)/2\), \(\lambda_2 = (s^2 - \bar x)/2\), truncated at 0.

na.rm

Logical; if TRUE, missing values are removed before fitting. If FALSE (default), missing values give an error.

object, digits, ..., level, parm, type, nsim, seed

Arguments of the methods: object is a "skellam_fit" object; parm and level as in confint; type in predict is "pmf" (default), "cdf" or "quantile", evaluated at x (quantiles at probabilities p); nsim and seed as in simulate.

p

Probabilities, for predict(type = "quantile").

Value

An object of class "skellam_fit", a list with components

estimate

Named vector c(lambda1 = , lambda2 = ).

vcov

2 x 2 covariance matrix of the estimates (NA on the boundary and for the moment method).

loglik

Log-likelihood at the estimates.

nobs

Number of observations used.

method

"mle" or "moments".

boundary

TRUE if one rate is estimated as 0.

evals

Number of log-likelihood evaluations (maximum likelihood).

x

The data used.

call

The matched call.

Methods are available for print, summary, coef, vcov, logLik (hence AIC and BIC), nobs, confint, predict and simulate.

Details

Maximum likelihood. At the maximum the fitted mean equals the sample mean, \(\hat\lambda_1 - \hat\lambda_2 = \bar{x}\), so the log-likelihood is maximised over \(\lambda_2\) alone with optimize, on the range that keeps both rates non-negative. The covariance matrix is the inverse of the observed information, computed from the analytic score.

Boundary estimates. A Skellam with two positive rates has variance \(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 \ge |\lambda_1 - \lambda_2|\). When the sample variance does not exceed the absolute sample mean, the maximum lies on the boundary, with one rate equal to 0 (a Poisson or a reflected Poisson): a sample of zeros gives \((0, 0)\), a constant sample \(c > 0\) gives \((c, 0)\). Standard errors do not exist there; the covariance matrix is then NA and the fit is flagged with boundary = TRUE and a warning.

Moments. The moment estimates are returned without a covariance matrix and serve mainly as a quick check or a starting point.

Confidence intervals are Wald intervals on the log scale, \(\exp(\log\hat\lambda \pm z\,\mathrm{se}/\hat\lambda)\), which keeps them positive; they are NA when the covariance matrix is.

References

Karlis, D. and Ntzoufras, I. (2009) Bayesian modelling of football outcomes: using the Skellam's distribution for the goal difference. IMA Journal of Management Mathematics 20(2), 133-145.

See also

skellam for the distribution functions, skellam.reg for regression on covariates.

Examples

set.seed(1)
x <- rpois(500, 6) - rpois(500, 4)
fit <- skellam.fit(x)
fit
#> Skellam distribution fitted by maximum likelihood (n = 500)
#> 
#>         Estimate Std. Error
#> lambda1    5.683     0.3126
#> lambda2    3.717     0.3063
#> 
#> log-likelihood -1268.513, AIC 2541.026
summary(fit)
#> 
#> Call:
#> skellam.fit(x = x)
#> 
#> Skellam distribution fitted by maximum likelihood (n = 500)
#> 
#>         Estimate Std. Error 2.5 % 97.5 %
#> lambda1    5.683     0.3126 5.102  6.330
#> lambda2    3.717     0.3063 3.163  4.368
#> 
#> Sample and fitted moments:
#>                   sample  fitted
#> mean             1.96600 1.96600
#> variance         9.36357 9.39958
#> skewness         0.04562 0.06822
#> excess kurtosis -0.21702 0.10639
#> 
#> var(x) - |mean(x)| = 7.398 (must be >= 0 for two positive rates)
#> log-likelihood -1268.513, AIC 2541.026, BIC 2549.455
coef(fit)
#>  lambda1  lambda2 
#> 5.682792 3.716792 
confint(fit)
#>            2.5 %   97.5 %
#> lambda1 5.101969 6.329738
#> lambda2 3.162510 4.368223
AIC(fit)
#> [1] 2541.026

# probabilities and quantities from the fitted distribution
predict(fit, x = -2:2)
#> [1] 0.05635807 0.08278187 0.10844110 0.12656940 0.13174771
predict(fit, x = 0, type = "cdf")
#> [1] 0.3166358

# the boundary: a constant sample is best fitted by a Poisson
skellam.fit(rep(3, 50))
#> Warning: the estimate lies on the boundary (a rate is 0): the sample variance does not exceed the absolute mean; standard errors are not available
#> Skellam distribution fitted by maximum likelihood (n = 50)
#> 
#>         Estimate Std. Error
#> lambda1        3         NA
#> lambda2        0         NA
#> 
#> log-likelihood -74.79613, AIC 153.5923
#> Estimate on the boundary: one rate is 0 (standard errors not available).
